papers.abstract: Active geo-localization (AGL) asks an agent to navigate a small aerial search grid and reach a target specified by an aerial image, a ground-level photograph, or text. Existing methods align the goal modalities well, but they keep the navigation state inside a large sequential Transformer and train with a dense distance reward that uses the hidden goal location. This paper proposes EAGLE, an Explicit spatial-belief Agent for Geo-Localization and Exploration. Offline training jointly optimizes a teacher-conditioned Swin branch and a context-free Swin student from the same randomly masked partial mosaics. The teacher branch attends to frozen full-scene context extracted by Qwen2.5-VL-7B, both branches receive masked-cell aerial-feature reconstruction and uncertainty supervision, while the student additionally distills stop-gradient feature predictions from the teacher. After distillation, Qwen, its cached context, and the teacher-attention branch are discarded. The retained student predicts cell-level aerial-feature embeddings and predictive uncertainty from partial observations alone. These predictions are combined with the modality-aligned goal embedding and a trajectory-derived visitation mask to construct the spatial belief tensor. The student is then frozen while a compact CNN actor-critic is optimized with PPO. EAGLE achieves state-of-the-art average success rates of 78.1%, 76.4%, and 76.8% on MASA, xBD zero-shot transfer, and the MM-GAG zero-shot aerial-goal split, respectively, without using a VLM or cached visual tokens at inference. Code will be made publicly available.
bullets: Addresses AGL state representation by replacing implicit sequential Transformer memory with explicit cell-level spatial beliefs.
Trains a Swin teacher–student system on masked aerial mosaics using reconstruction, uncertainty supervision, and feature distillation from frozen Qwen2.5-VL context.
Combines student predictions, the aligned goal embedding, and visitation history into a spatial belief tensor.
Freezes the student and trains a compact CNN actor–critic with PPO for navigation.
Reports average success rates of 78.1% on MASA, 76.4% on xBD zero-shot transfer, and 76.8% on the MM-GAG zero-shot aerial-goal split; inference uses no VLM or cached visual tokens.

Both branches receive masked-cell aerial-feature reconstruction and branch-specific heteroscedastic supervision. The student also matches detached teacher features. Stage 2 removes the teacher path and trains the CNN policy with a frozen student tracker.

Figure 1: Multi-modal active geo-localization. An aerial image, ground photograph, or text query identifies the same hidden target. The agent observes one local aerial patch at a time and uses four-neighbor moves to reach the target within a fixed budget.

Table 1: Main results. Success ratio (%) by Manhattan start-goal distance and dataset. For MM-GAG, the aerial-goal block includes the full aerial-goal comparison after omitting Random. The ground-image and text blocks compare EAGLE with GOMAA-Geo and GeoExplorer.

Table 2: Ablation summary (average success ratio, %). MMGAG averages all three goal modalities. The w/o distillation variant uses student-only Stage 1. The other variants remove Ut and its coverage bonus or remove Vt during PPO and evaluation.

papers.selection_reason: Active geo-localization agent navigating to multimodal-specified goals with explicit spatial belief; fits goal-conditioned and vision-language navigation.
papers.title: From Sequence to Space: Explicit Spatial Belief with Vision-Language Distillation for Active Geo-Localization
papers.tldr: EAGLE enables active geo-localization with an explicit spatial belief map distilled from a vision-language teacher, achieving strong zero-shot performance without VLM use at inference.

papers.abstract: A robot must choose an action before it can see the outcome. In a recorded demonstration, later camera frames show what happened after the robot moved. Hindsight Self-Distillation (HSD) uses these later frames to teach a policy what to extract from current images. During training, a teacher sees both the current and later frames, while a student sees the current frames. They share a visual encoder and an action predictor. Each branch summarizes its images with a small set of feature vectors. These visual summaries supply all visual input to the action predictor. The teacher learns from demonstrated actions. For each noisy action sequence, the student learns from either the demonstration or the teacher's denoising prediction. It also learns to match the teacher's visual summaries. We analyze which aspects of the teacher's predictions the student can recover from its inputs. At deployment, the student encodes the current images once and reuses its summaries at every denoising step. HSD achieves average success rates of 98.50\% on LIBERO and 92.31\% on RoboTwin 2.0.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of choosing actions before their outcomes are visible.
A teacher sees current and later frames, while a student sees only current frames; both share visual and action components.
The student learns from demonstrated actions or the teacher’s denoising predictions and matches the teacher’s visual summaries.
At deployment, the student computes current-image features once and reuses them throughout denoising.
Reports average success rates of 98.50% on LIBERO and 92.31% on RoboTwin 2.0.

papers.selection_reason: Robot policy learning from demonstrations via hindsight self-distillation; fits imitation learning and visuomotor control.
papers.title: Hindsight Self-Distillation: Teaching Robots to Act from the Present
papers.tldr: Hindsight Self-Distillation trains robots to act from current images by using future observations as privileged guidance during training.

papers.abstract: Large-scale applications of lifelong multi-agent path finding (LMAPF) call for computationally inexpensive movement decisions under changing traffic conditions and across varied layouts. We propose a navigation policy in which a convolutional network computes a shared spatial field over the map once per timestep and a compact goal-conditioned operator derives agents' movement preferences. The complete policy is trained end-to-end using average-reward reinforcement learning with throughput as the reward, without planner demonstrations or a separate online path planner. For structured and unstructured layouts, we train one policy per class on pools of small maps and deploy each without retraining on larger, unseen layouts and agent populations. Across six layouts with 10,000 agents, our policies achieve throughput comparable to or higher than the strongest evaluated baselines. The proposed method has an average execution time below 10 ms per step, more than an order of magnitude faster than several established planners.
bullets: Targets scalable movement decisions under changing traffic and varied map layouts.
Computes one shared convolutional spatial field per timestep, then derives compact goal-conditioned movement preferences for each agent.
Trains end-to-end with average-reward reinforcement learning using throughput, without planner demonstrations or a separate online planner.
Policies trained on small-map pools transfer to larger unseen layouts and populations; across six layouts with 10,000 agents, throughput is comparable to or better than evaluated baselines.
Runs in under 10 ms per step on average, though policies are trained separately for structured and unstructured layout classes.

papers.selection_reason: Learned goal-conditioned navigation policy for large-scale multi-agent path finding fits robot navigation.
papers.title: Reinforcement Learning for Large-Scale Lifelong Multi-Agent Path Finding with Shared Spatial Fields
papers.tldr: A shared spatial-field reinforcement-learning policy enables fast, planner-free lifelong multi-agent navigation that generalizes to larger maps and agent populations.

papers.abstract: We study causal error-feedback coefficients as design variables for model quantization. Modeling instantaneous quantization errors as independent, zero-mean variables with a common fixed variance, we formulated a metric-dependent trace problem for designing feedback coefficients. The formulation resembles fixed-order GPTQ/LDLQ feedback and supports Jacobian-aware designs that account for downstream error propagation. For a positive-definite metric $\boldsymbol{H}$, we prove that the joint rotation-feedback trace minimum is $n\det(\boldsymbol{H})^{1/n}$ and present an attaining pair using the geometric mean decomposition. Experiments on synthetic networks, trained MLPs, and language models show benefits from downstream-sensitive feedback, but also reveal that trace optimality need not improve finite-level performance. Small QAT experiments further illustrate direct loss-driven feedback tuning with fixed or trainable network weights.
bullets: Models quantization errors as independent, zero-mean variables with fixed variance and optimizes metric-dependent feedback coefficients.
Develops Jacobian-aware designs that account for how errors propagate through downstream layers.
Proves that the joint rotation-feedback trace minimum for positive-definite H is n det(H)^(1/n), with an attaining construction via geometric mean decomposition.
Experiments across synthetic networks, MLPs, and language models find benefits from downstream-sensitive feedback, but trace optimality does not consistently improve finite-level performance.
Small QAT studies demonstrate direct loss-driven feedback tuning with fixed or trainable weights.

papers.selection_reason: Model quantization with error-feedback design directly targets efficient inference and memory reduction.
papers.title: Revisiting Error Feedback for Model Quantization
papers.tldr: Revisiting error-feedback design as an optimization problem shows how to minimize downstream quantization error, while highlighting that trace-optimal designs may not yield better finite-level accuracy.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have achieved strong performance on diverse vision-language tasks, but their computational demands limit deployment under constrained budgets, particularly on edge devices. Many works focus on Knowledge Distillation (KD) and try to transfer knowledge from powerful teacher models to students. In addition to reducing model size, visual token compression provides a complementary route to efficiency, but introduces mismatched visual token counts that complicate direct token-wise knowledge transfer. To mitigate this, we propose DVTR-KD, a knowledge distillation framework based on \textbf{D}ense \textbf{V}isual \textbf{T}oken \textbf{R}econstruction, which reconstructs the teacher's dense visual tokens from the student's compressed tokens. We reconstruct visual states after the final LLM layer and at the input to an intermediate layer identified as important for visual-information readout. At the intermediate layer, reconstruction is supervised through the teacher's response predictions rather than by direct token-wise KL or MSE matching. An auxiliary attention-readout loss complements this response-level supervision by aligning how the student and the original teacher integrate contextual information when predicting responses. Evaluations on diverse benchmarks demonstrate that DVTR-KD improves the performance of token-compressed students while retaining the inference efficiency afforded by visual token compression.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of knowledge transfer when visual token compression creates mismatched teacher and student token counts.
Reconstructs teacher visual states after the final LLM layer and before an important intermediate layer.
Uses response-level supervision at the intermediate layer instead of direct token-wise KL or MSE matching.
Adds an attention-readout loss to align contextual information integration during response prediction.
Evaluations across diverse benchmarks show improved performance for token-compressed students while retaining inference efficiency.

papers.selection_reason: Knowledge distillation with visual token compression for MLLMs; addresses efficiency and multimodal model improvement.
papers.title: DVTR-KD: Distilling Vision-Language Models via Intermediate Visual Token Reconstruction
papers.tldr: DVTR-KD distills vision-language models by reconstructing dense teacher visual tokens from compressed student tokens, improving compressed-student performance while preserving token-efficiency benefits.

papers.abstract: GUI grounding enables web agents to translate natural-language instructions into actionable interface locations. However, dense layouts and small, visually similar controls can lead models toward plausible but incorrect elements, while refinement around a single prediction may leave alternative targets unexplored. We propose the Multi-Hypothesis Verification Framework (MHVF) for training-free GUI grounding. It combines multi-hypothesis exploration with local visual verification using a single pretrained vision-language model. To explore alternative targets, MHVF constructs spatial hypotheses from multiple full-screen predictions and examines the corresponding regions through zoomed re-localization. To resolve ambiguity among the resulting candidates, it verifies their agreement with the instruction in marked local views. Verification scores then guide a second round of local search and rank candidates retained from both search levels for final selection. Experiments with five general-purpose and GUI-specific models across eight benchmark settings demonstrate improvements in grounding accuracy in most settings. MHVF improves UI-Venus-Ground-7B by 4.3 and 2.1 percentage points on Mind2Web and VisualWebBench, respectively, and raises Qwen2.5-VL-7B's accuracy on ScreenSpot-Pro from 23.6% to 53.6%.
bullets: Addresses errors from dense layouts and visually similar controls, where single-prediction refinement can miss the correct target.
Uses one pretrained vision-language model to generate full-screen hypotheses, zoom into candidate regions, and verify instruction–region agreement.
Verification scores guide a second local-search round and rank candidates from both search stages.

Across five models and eight benchmark settings, MHVF improves accuracy in most settings; examples include +4.3 and +2.1 points for UI-Venus-Ground-7B and 23.6% to 53.6% for Qwen2.5-VL-7B on ScreenSpot-Pro.

The lower panels illustrate verification and local refinement for “add new tab,” where H4 is reopened and H4.1 yields the final click.
